title: Why the First Lesson Sets the Tone
brief: Open by explaining why day one matters so much for establishing the classroom environment. Draw on the source's repeated emphasis that establishing routines helps students become more well-behaved and autonomous learners, and that classroom management and self-management routines are foundational to how a class functions throughout a course. Explain that the choices a teacher makes on day one—how the room is arranged, how transitions are handled, how students are called upon—send signals that shape student behaviour for weeks to come. Keep the focus practical and forward-looking, framing the rest of the unit as a toolkit the new teacher can use immediately.

title: Setting Up the Room and Establishing Routines
brief: Cover the physical and procedural groundwork a teacher lays before students arrive and in the opening minutes of lesson one. Draw on the source's discussion of classroom set-up, including how room arrangement affects what activities are possible and how teachers can use available resources to adapt their space to their teaching context. Bring in the source's treatment of classroom routines—specifically how teachers can have students help with classroom routines—as a way to build ownership from day one. Also draw on the source's point that managing transitions between activities can be difficult, and introduce simple transition signals (such as a verbal cue or a song) as a routine worth establishing immediately. Exclude deep discussion of learning stations, which belongs to a later unit.

title: Learning Every Student's Name
brief: Focus entirely on the practical challenge of learning and using student names quickly, treating it as a classroom management and relationship-building priority. Draw on the source's discussion of how teachers call on students to share information and how teachers can get more than one student to answer each question, framing name-learning as the prerequisite for those techniques. Use the source's concept of student-centered learning and encouraging student output to argue that a teacher who knows names can distribute participation more equitably from the very first lesson. Offer concrete name-learning strategies that fit within the source's framework of short, varied activities—such as name cards, repetition games, and seating charts—without making any claims about research.

title: Icebreakers That Double as Language Practice
brief: Present a set of concrete icebreaker activities that simultaneously introduce students to each other and generate genuine language use. Draw directly on the source's activity formats: students asking each other questions on their papers and writing down classmates' answers (a pair-work information-exchange format); students brainstorming ideas and responding to survey results in whole-class discussion; and small groups presenting findings to the whole class. Frame each activity type in terms of the interaction modes the source identifies—pairs, small groups, whole-class discussion, individuals speaking in front of the class—so the new teacher understands how to vary the social dynamic across a single lesson. Emphasise that icebreakers should require students to produce language, not just listen, connecting to the source's concern about giving students opportunities to freely produce language.

title: Reducing First-Day Anxiety Through Encouragement and Clear Expectations
brief: Address the emotional dimension of day one by focusing on how a teacher's feedback style and communication of expectations can lower student anxiety. Draw on the source's description of a teacher who gives positive feedback to students when they answer questions correctly and who manages off-task students without disrupting the flow of the lesson, presenting these as anxiety-reducing techniques any new teacher can adopt. Bring in the source's discussion of wait time—including the advantages and disadvantages of long and short wait times—as a concrete decision the teacher makes that signals to students whether the classroom is a safe place to attempt answers. Also draw on the source's point about concept-checking questions as a low-stakes way to check understanding without putting individual students on the spot.

title: A Sample Day-One Lesson Plan
brief: Synthesise the unit by walking the reader through a complete, annotated sample lesson plan for a first class. Structure the plan using the lesson phases implied throughout the source: a warm-up or opening activity, a middle phase with varied interaction modes, and a wrap-up. Draw on the source's lesson plan template concept and its action-plan prompt—design a lesson, share it with colleagues, get feedback, revise, then try it—to frame lesson planning as an iterative process rather than a one-time task. Incorporate the unit's key elements: a room-setup note, a name-learning activity, at least one icebreaker that produces language, a transition signal, a positive-feedback moment, and a brief wrap-up that includes movement, as the source describes teachers doing at the end of lessons with younger learners. Close with a short reflection prompt drawn from the source's 'reflect on what went well and what you might do differently' guidance.
